S10281800108d.topic: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh roughly a billion tonnes on Earth.
S10281800108d.title: A Teaspoon of Neutron Star Weighs a Billion Tonnes #shorts
S10281800108d.description:
A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tonnes on Earth. Follow for more weird science, explained calmly.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S10281800108d.narration: A teaspoon of neutron star weighs about a billion tonnes. Let's unpack that. A neutron star is what's left when a massive star runs out of fuel and collapses. Its core crushes down until protons and electrons are squeezed into neutrons. Now picture about one and a half times the Sun's mass. Packed into a ball roughly 20 kilometers across. Roughly the size of a city. Your teaspoon of sugar weighs about five grams. This one weighs about two and a half times as much as all the people on Earth combined. Mount Everest, by comparison, is roughly 160 times heavier than that teaspoon. Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times a second. Wait, it gets weirder: they can sweep beams of radio waves like lighthouses. It's just matter squeezed beyond anything on Earth. Mind-bending, right? Follow for more weird science.

S102819104db3.topic: Daniel Kahneman's planning fallacy: we keep believing the next project will go faster than the last one, even when it never has.
S102819104db3.title: The Clockmaker Who Always Promises Friday #shorts
S102819104db3.description:
A quiet allegory about the planning fallacy, an idea Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky described in their research and that Kahneman explores in Thinking, Fast and Slow. Some other studies he cites there, such as priming and ego-depletion work, later failed to replicate, but the planning fallacy has held up well.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S102819104db3.narration: In the town of Low Fen, the old clockmaker promises every clock will be finished by Friday. Every clock, every Friday, for forty years. Mist curls through her open window as she sketches tiny gears with quick, hopeful strokes. The last clock took three months, not three days. Her apprentice only smiles and pours the tea. She is certain this one will be different. Daniel Kahneman called this the planning fallacy: we keep believing our next task will go faster than the last, even when it never has. An idea from Thinking, Fast and Slow.

S10281910472e.topic: Daniel Kahneman: losing something tends to hurt about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good (loss aversion; the exact ratio varies between studies).
S10281910472e.title: Why Humans Hoarded Dead Cables: Loss Aversion #shorts
S10281910472e.description:
Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, a pattern called loss aversion, though the exact ratio varies between studies. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied it, and Kahneman explains the idea in Thinking, Fast and Slow; some other effects he cites later failed to replicate. Thanks to Daniel Kahneman for the book this short is based on.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S10281910472e.narration: Museum label, year 2126. Our ancestors refused to throw away a single sock. Why? Losing something tends to hurt roughly twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good. Find twenty dollars and enjoy it for a moment. Lose twenty dollars and it lingers all day. Specimens show drawers full of dead cables, unused gym passes, and cracked mugs kept just in case. Curators debate the exact ratio, since studies vary. The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named this loss aversion. Kahneman explored it in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow. Please keep your hands away from the sock.

S10281912f08b.topic: Daniel Kahneman: losing something tends to hurt about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good (loss aversion; the exact ratio varies between studies).
S10281912f08b.title: Why losing a twenty-dollar bill stings more than finding one #shorts
S10281912f08b.description:
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky described loss aversion, the tendency for losses to feel roughly twice as strong as equal gains, though the exact ratio varies between studies. This Short retells the idea from Kahneman's book Thinking, Fast and Slow; note that some other studies he cites later failed to replicate.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S10281912f08b.narration: Historians of 2126 still puzzle over one habit from our era. Losing things hurt us far more than gaining them pleased us. Lose a twenty-dollar bill, and the sting lingers all afternoon. Find one, and the joy fades by dinner. Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky measured this in experiments. Losses often felt roughly twice as painful as equal gains felt good, though the exact ratio varied between studies. So people kept unused gym memberships, broken phones and jobs they disliked, just to avoid the feeling of losing. Our curators find this baffling. The idea comes from Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper on prospect theory, "Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk". Kahneman later popularized it in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).

S102819125a27.topic: Marshall Rosenberg believed that behind every harsh criticism there is an unmet need the person doesn't know how to ask for.
S102819125a27.title: Why Harsh Words Hide a Need Nobody Asked For #shorts
S102819125a27.description:
Marshall Rosenberg's approach in his book Nonviolent Communication holds that harsh criticism often masks an unmet need. It is a communication method rather than a settled scientific theory, retold here as a quiet fairytale.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S102819125a27.narration: In the trench where the sea forgets the sun, every harsh word leaves a spark. Old Nell the anglerfish hangs her lantern and watches them fall. Tonight a young moth tumbles down, flinging sparks: 'You never listen. You're useless.' Nell tilts her light. Behind the sparks she sees a small, tired wing folding. Nobody ever taught the moth how to ask. So Nell says softly, 'You wanted someone to notice you, didn't you?' The moth's wings slow. The sparks go dark, one by one. Marshall Rosenberg believed every harsh criticism hides an unmet need the person does not know how to ask for. That is the core of his approach in Nonviolent Communication.

S1028191788b0.narration: Historians of the 2120s are baffled by a habit from our era: keeping old chargers in a drawer for years. They also kept unopened subscriptions, cracked mugs, and shoeboxes of cables. Asked why, the answer was often simple: letting go felt like losing something. Researchers call this loss aversion. In classic experiments by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, losing a sum of money hurt roughly twice as much as gaining the same sum felt good. The exact ratio varies between studies, so treat the number as a rough guide. Your brain tends to weigh losses more heavily than gains. The idea is explored in Daniel Kahneman's book Thinking, Fast and Slow.

S10281959fd99.narration: In Lantern Hollow, every sharp word is a letter folded the wrong way. Mira, a blue cat with a silver bell, sits on the mill wall each evening. Below her, a neighbor shouts at a closed gate. Mira doesn't hiss. She waits, tail curled, listening past the anger for what is really missing: rest, respect, someone to notice. Marshall Rosenberg taught that behind every harsh criticism sits an unmet need the speaker never learned to ask for. An idea from Nonviolent Communication.

S10282008806b.topic: Daniel Kahneman: losing something tends to hurt about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good (loss aversion; the exact ratio varies between studies).
S10282008806b.title: Why Losing Hurts Twice as Much (Kahneman) #psychology #science
S10282008806b.description:
Daniel Kahneman, in Thinking, Fast and Slow, describes loss aversion: losses tend to weigh roughly twice as much as equal gains, though the exact ratio varies between studies. This idea rests on strong research by Kahneman and Amos Tversky, while some priming and ego-depletion findings the book cites later failed to replicate.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S10282008806b.narration: You find twenty dollars and feel mildly pleased. You lose twenty dollars and feel mildly ruined. Welcome to a documentary on this strange human habit. Losses tend to hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good, though the exact ratio varies between studies. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky identified this pattern in their 1979 prospect theory paper, and it became known as loss aversion. Kahneman later popularized the idea in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow. Psychologists and economists still debate why we keep this lopsided ledger. Evolutionary explanations are plausible, but they remain unproven, and the size of the effect changes with context.
